title: Apollo 11 Daylight Launch
desc: Ten seconds of grain-rich 1969 KSC tracking-camera film — the SVX2 codec's hardest realistic input — decoded byte-exactly at a locked 30 fps.
keys: No controls — the 300-frame loop plays continuously.
pageDesc: An 8 Mbit Fast HiROM SNES cartridge playing 300 frames of 16 mm Apollo 11 launch film through the SVX2 codec, with the whole loop byte-checked against a host oracle in the build gate.
heading: Apollo 11 Daylight Launch
lede: Ten seconds of real 16 mm KSC tracking-camera film from 16 July 1969 — heavy grain, bright continuous exhaust, smoke against sky. Deliberately chosen as the hardest realistic input the SVX2 codec will ever be handed, and still presented in 300 frames per 600 VBlanks with zero deadline slips.
keysHtml: No input — the 300-frame loop plays continuously. Every frame is decoded from the cartridge in real time; nothing is pre-rendered to VRAM.
doc:
Why this clip is the hard case

The companion SVX2 FastROM reel plays Artemis I — a night launch, mostly black frames whose sensor noise an H.264 derivative had already smoothed before our converter ever saw it. Its 31–57% compression ratios are a best case for “real footage.” This cartridge is the opposite, and was picked to be: daylight film grain, a bright continuous exhaust flame, and a smoke plume of fine high-frequency edges. Measured cost of that hardness under the shipping codec: +5.29 ratio points at the quality-first Floyd–Steinberg default (57.04% → 62.33%), and +19.80 points under Bayer (33.49% → 53.29%).

Film grain decorrelates consecutive frames enough to undercut the assumption an interframe codec rests on. The clearest symptom: across seek intervals of 15, 30, 60 and 120 frames the Floyd stream varies by only 213 bytes (837,899 → 837,686) — on this content a delta packet costs almost as much as a fresh keyframe. On the same corpus, intraframe-only gallery LZSS (a comparison baseline, not a shipping path) actually comes out smaller than interframe SVX2 at Floyd, 801,766 vs 837,686 bytes. That never happened on the night leg, where SVX2 won at both dithers.

What the cartridge contains

Frames300 (10 seconds at 30 fps)
DitherFloyd–Steinberg, 31.98 dB PSNR
CodecSVX2 — PackBits keyframes plus replacement/copy delta spans
Packed stream848,527 B = 837,028 delta packets + 8,465 seek keyframes (3, K=120) + 3,034 loop delta
Raw equivalent1,344,000 B indexed (300 × 4,480)
Cartridge8 Mbit (1 MiB) Fast HiROM — the stream begins at bank $C1

Cadence, measured both ways

The metric is the one the 60 fps work established — presented frames per 600 VBlanks — so this content is directly comparable to the Artemis figures. It was recorded for a slow-ROM build and a FastROM build of the same source:

build      presented   vblanks   per 600   slips
slow ROM         300       600       300       0
FastROM          300       600       300       0

Both hold a locked 30 fps with zero deadline slips. The hardest realistic input the decoder has been handed does not cost it a single frame — the +5.3 ratio points show up as cartridge bytes, not as dropped frames, because a larger packet still stages and decodes inside the 2-VBlank budget.

Byte-exact, and provably so

A separate self-test build decodes all 300 frames with the screen force-blanked and checks each one against a Fletcher 16 oracle computed by the host encoder, then compares the final frame byte for byte, then decodes the wrap-around delta that closes the loop and re-checks frame 0. A frame-zero-only check would pass on a decoder that corrupted every delta; this one cannot. That sweep is bit-serial and costs roughly 37 seconds of console time, so it belongs to the build gate — the cartridge you are running goes straight to its title card and starts playing in about three seconds.

The gate carries a negative control, because a checksum that cannot fail proves nothing: flipping one byte of the packed stream (offset 400,000, 0x78 → 0x79) makes the whole-loop check reject the cartridge. The Verify fidelity button above runs the shipped ROM's own assert — two complete playback loops with zero decode failures. The build is also -verify-machineinstrs clean, and renders one identical picture across six power-on entropy settings, so nothing here inherits PPU state the ROM never sets.

Source: NASA / Kennedy Space Center, item KSC-19690716-MH-NAS01-0001, “Video – Apollo 11 Pre-Launch and Launch,” date_created 1969-07-16. Interval 00:56:50–00:57:00 of the 3,634-second master — post-ignition vertical ascent, after the burned-in countdown-clock overlay and camera-ID tags have scrolled out of frame. Video stream only; audio discarded entirely. Lanczos to 80×45, padded, retimed 59.94 → 30 fps by frame selection with no optical flow. NASA-produced 1969 archival footage, not subject to copyright for US distribution under NASA's media guidelines.
